data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on Popper's own terms as a methodological rule based on the asymmetry of risk, not as an inductive inference of future probability.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If it can be demonstrated that preferring the better-corroborated theory logically entails a belief in its future success (induction).","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If Popper explicitly stated that acting on corroboration requires assigning a higher probability to the theory.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the choice of the better-corroborated theory is shown to be irrational unless one assumes the uniformity of nature.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Popper distinguishes between the logical status of a theory (which cannot be made probable by past tests) and the rational decision to act upon it. The mechanism relies on the 'asymmetry of risk': rejecting a well-corroborated theory in favor of a less-tested one exposes the agent to a higher risk of immediate falsification without any compensating gain in informational content. Therefore, choosing the better-corroborated theory is a non-inductive, critical preference for the theory that has withstood the most severe attempts at refutation, minimizing the likelihood of error in the present moment without guaranteeing future success.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
